segments.text: In my town, nobody is allowed to sleep.
The mayor made it the law last year.
He says sleep is a waste of time.
He hasn't slept in 40 years, and he's proud of it.
So beds are against the law now.
The furniture store only sells chairs.
At night, the police shine flashlights into every window.
If your eyes are closed, you pay $100.
And every night at midnight, the mayor goes live
on every TV and phone in town.
It's called the wake check, and you can't turn it off.
He picks one house and video calls it live.
Houses with the lights off get picked first.
If you look sleepy, you pay.
So nobody turns their lights off anymore.
Everyone is tired all the time.
My sister Ava is six, and she's the most tired of all.
Eli, I'm so tired.
She cries every night.
I promised Ava I'd find a way to help her sleep.
On my bus, a kid in the very back
eats a burger every morning, and I know this kid.
He helped me get my very first burger.
But when I said hi, he just stared at me
like he'd never seen me before.
Nobody has ever heard him talk.
Nobody even knows his name.
So everyone calls him Random Kid.
Hey, Random Kid, say something.
Everyone laughs.
He just keeps chewing.
Then one morning, he took a big bite and hummed.
Hmm, hmm.
And every kid on the bus fell asleep, including me.
I woke up six hours later in the bus garage.
We'd all slept through school.
The driver had headphones on, and he
was too tired to notice us.
Random Kid was still awake finishing his burger,
and I felt better than I had all year.
That's why he never talks.
His voice puts people to sleep.
That gave me an idea.
The wake check is the one time every night when the whole town
hears the same thing.
And houses with the lights off get picked first.
So if Random Kid's house was the only dark one,
the mayor would call him, and the whole town
would hear his voice.
Everyone would fall asleep at once, even the police.
Nobody would have to pay.
I just hoped his voice would work through a TV.
That afternoon, I followed Random Kid home
and explained my plan.
I told him about Ava, too.
He didn't say anything, but he nodded.
That night at midnight, every light in town was on,
except his.
Ooh, lights off.
Let's see who's sleeping tonight.
The mayor called Random Kid live
with the whole town watching.
Are you sleeping?
Say something.
And Random Kid, the kid who never talks, opened his mouth.
Don't stay away from Tuna.
Don't go to bed.
I'll make you cup and coffee for your head.
The mayor fell asleep on live TV.
The police fell asleep in their cars.
Ava fell asleep before he even finished.
I had earplugs in, so I stayed awake and saw it all.
Then I took one out, just to hear his voice.
Bad idea.
I was asleep in two seconds.
The next morning, the whole town
woke up at the same time.
Nobody had felt that good in a year,
especially the mayor.
That was his first sleep in 40 years.
Why didn't anybody remind me how good sleep feels?
That same day, he made sleeping OK again.
Now the wake check is the sleep check.
Every night at nine, the mayor calls Random Kid,
and the whole town falls asleep together.
Ava sleeps 12 hours a night now,
but I still don't know Random Kid's name.
I asked him once.
He opened his mouth to answer,
and I woke up in the bus garage.
